title: Paving the way for sustainable employment for women
content:
• Focus

    IECD reading

    • IECD reading

    Access to the labour market is one of the main barriers to women’s social integration and economic empowerment: globally, only 47% of women achieve this, compared with 72% of men (International Labour Organisation).
    Transforming what is learnt on training courses into skills sought after in the labour market is essential, but it is not enough. For women to be able to truly seize career opportunities, an environment conducive to their entry into the labour market must be created: women with greater self-confidence and employability, a supportive social circle, and committed public and private sector stakeholders. 

    Engaging the support network of young women to strengthen their ability to choose their career path

title: Talent mobility: unlocking prosperity in the Mediterranean?
content:
• Focus

    IECD reading

    • IECD reading

    The Mediterranean does not lack talent. It lacks bridges.

    More than one in two people are under the age of 30 in the Middle East and North Africa. This represents an extraordinary pool of energy, skills and ambition, at a time when several countries around the Mediterranean are facing ageing populations and labour shortages in key sectors.

    Indeed, companies on both shores of the Mediterranean are struggling to recruit in healthcare, construction, energy, hospitality, logistics and services. Yet nearly one in three young people remains unemployed.

    This paradox challenges us to rethink our ability to better connect young people’s skills with the needs of Mediterranean economies.

    What if the real challenge was ultimately not a lack of opportunities or talent, but our collective ability to build bridges between the two?

    Reducing mobility to a migration issue alone would be a mistake. It is also a matter of economic development, training and regional cooperation. When it is prepared, chosen and secured, mobility can address both young people’s aspirations and businesses’ needs.

title: Conversation with our partner Accor Heartist Solidarity
content:
• Conversation with our partner Accor Heartist Solidarity

    • Trust is the foundation. The ability to maintain regular dialogue about the project, including when addressing more complex or sensitive issues. And this trust must exist at every level: on the ground, between hotel teams and project staff, as well as between our respective headquarters.

    This strong relationship has enabled the partnership to take root and grow over time across several countries. What began in 2013 with support for around thirty Karen young people in Thailand has evolved into a regional programme benefiting around 800 people across Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam.

    How does this partnership fit within Accor Group’s CSR strategy?

    This partnership is fully aligned with one of the four “Extra Mile” pillars of our CSR strategy, which focuses on promoting the sustainable professional integration of people who face significant barriers to employment.

    Each year, IECD’s programmes provide vocational training to several hundred beneficiaries across a range of professions, helping them broaden their opportunities and build lasting careers.

title: Conversation with our partner the French Development Agency in Madagascar
content:
• Conversation with our partner Accor Heartist Solidarity

    • AFD has been supporting Madagascar and its people for more than 70 years. While the country’s economic and social vulnerabilities are deeply rooted, we have adapted our operations to take into account the impacts of climate change and chronic underinvestment in public services.

    As France’s public development bank, our role is to support the authorities in designing fiscally sustainable public policies that deliver tangible benefits for the population, while also helping to finance their implementation.

    Madagascar is currently facing an exceptional situation: its main macroeconomic and social indicators are deteriorating, whereas, outside countries affected by conflict, these indicators are generally improving. Together with the international financial institutions and our European partners, our ambition is to support this transition so that Madagascar can ultimately return to sustainable growth and provide quality public services across the country.

title: Conversation with our partner the AnBer Foundation
content:
• Conversation with our partner Accor Heartist Solidarity

    • The AnBer Foundation has been supporting IECD for several years because your organisation is recognised, reliable, and deeply committed to working with the most vulnerable populations. What we particularly value is IECD’s ability to combine a long-term vision with operational efficiency, by developing concrete solutions tailored to local realities. Your approach, focused on training, professional integration, and economic development, aligns with our belief: giving everyone the means to become an actor in their own future.
    We also share the same standards of quality, monitoring, and project evaluation, which are essential in our role as a foundation.

    Supporting projects in such different contexts has taught us to be flexible and humble. We have strengthened our conviction that there is no single solution, but rather responses that must be built as closely as possible to local realities. This has also led us to place even greater importance on the quality of field actors, their adaptability, and their local anchoring.

title: From exclusion to inclusion: innovative pathways into careers in the hospitality and catering industry
content:
• Focus

    IECD reading

    • IECD reading

    For young people in socio-economic vulnerability, accessing sustainable employment is a real challenge.

    Addressing this challenge by offering genuine pathways to inclusion means investing in comprehensive programmes that combine technical training, human support, and workplace immersion.

    On the labour market, two realities coexist: NEETs, who represent nearly 20% of 15–24-year-olds and are neither in employment, education nor training; and businesses in labour-short sectors such as hospitality and catering, which face significant recruitment needs, with a projected workforce gap estimated at 18% by 2035 (WTTC, 2025).

    Bringing these two sides together may seem obvious, but in reality it remains difficult. Companies struggle to recruit candidates who are both operationally ready and comfortable with the relational demands of the sector, while these young people do not always have access to the training and support that would enable them to develop these skills.

    Pathways designed to address a dual challenge

title: One Health Summit: rethinking health across all life
content:
• Focus

    IECD reading

    • IECD reading

    In the face of escalating health, environmental, and food crises, the One Health approach is emerging as an essential response. Gathered in Lyon on April 6 and 7, public and private stakeholders reaffirmed the urgent need for coordinated action based on prevention, international cooperation, and the breaking down of sectoral silos.

    Global health: interconnected by nature 

    Human health cannot be considered in isolation from the health of animals and ecosystems. Today, approximately 60% of emerging infectious diseases originate in animals, and 75% of emerging human diseases come from animals. Each year, around five new diseases appear, three of which are zoonotic in origin (Ebola, COVID-19). In a world where 811 million people go to bed hungry and over 20% of global livestock production losses are disease-related, the One Health approach seeks to anticipate and prevent crises by fostering collaboration across disciplines—medicine, veterinary health, agronomy, ecology—and across regions. 

    From dialogue to action: transforming systems

title: In Argenteuil (France), a new place to bring out young people’s talents: “Excellence within everyone’s reach.”
content:
• Focus

    IECD reading

    • IECD reading

    Reynhald Le Baron, cabinetmaker and marquetry artisan, mentoring a young person from the local youth employment service (Mission Locale) in the making of a draughts board.

    In France, more than 75,000 young people leave the school system without a qualification each year. From an early age, some struggle to stay engaged with school, while many teenagers and young adults face difficulties in finding their place and building their future (Apprentis d’Auteuil).

    In the city of Argenteuil, a collective project to restore young people’s confidence 

    In Argenteuil (located in the Paris region), where 41% of the population is under 30, these challenges take on a particular significance (INSEE). For more than two years, IECD, in collaboration with its partners, in particular the City of Argenteuil, DYS CARE, and L’Outil en Main, has taken on the challenge of restoring young people’s confidence in their talents and skills, helping them move towards a chosen career path and sustainable social and professional integration.

title: RELIEEF Bootcamps: supporting youth towards action and professional independence
content:
• Focus

    IECD reading

    • IECD reading

    Facing the challenges of graduate employment in Central Africa, the RELIEEF project (Strengthening Women’s Employment and Entrepreneurship Opportunities) is rolling out a series of insertion, employability, and entrepreneurship bootcamps across its four operating countries: Cameroon, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the Republic of the Congo.

    In a region where nearly 60% of the population is under 25 (United Nations) and access to decent employment remains a major challenge, RELIEEF Bootcamps address this issue by offering short, intensive, and practical programmes that combine personal support, skills development, and real-world experience. The goal: to enable every young person—particularly young women—to define, assert, and realise their professional ambitions.

    RELIEEF Bootcamps were born from a simple observation: despite efforts in training, many graduates struggle to enter the workforce due to a lack of personalised guidance and direct links with the professional world. These intensive, multi-day programmes therefore aim to accelerate the transition to action, build self-confidence, and foster initiative.
creator: Florence Dominique
